headline: The yen broke to a six-month low against the dollar after a reflationist adviser inside Japan's prime ministerial circle conceded a September Bank of Japan hike and quarterly rises to 1.25% by January - USD/JPY fell 0.97% to 154.71, EUR/JPY 0.91% and AUD/JPY 0.79%, while Asian equities rallied. Crude rose about a percent, Brent to 97.42, after OPEC+ paused its output increases for October and Hormuz throughput fell to its lowest since May. The AfD took 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt on a preliminary official count and European markets shrugged. US equity and bond markets are shut for Labor Day, so none of it prices until Tuesday - the same morning Canada's C$27.6bn counter-tariffs take effect.
client_frame_short: The question worth pre-empting this week is not about jobs or oil. It is **why every major central bank is suddenly pointed the same direction, upward**. The Federal Reserve is priced at a 57% chance of raising rates on 16 September and at exactly zero chance of cutting at any meeting through March 2027. A Reuters poll expects the European Central Bank to raise on Thursday. And this morning an adviser to Japan's prime minister - a self-described reflationist, meaning a dove - conceded the Bank of Japan will hike this month and keep going quarterly to 1.25% by January. Japan was the world's last source of nearly free money. That era is closing, and the yen just moved to a six-month high to say so.
client_frame:
The frame that will serve you best this week is the one your clients have not heard yet: for the first time in this cycle, all three of the world's major central banks are pointed in the same direction, and that direction is up. Most clients still carry a mental model in which the next move in interest rates is downward, because that was the story for most of the last two years. That model is now wrong by direction, and it is worth correcting deliberately rather than letting a client discover it from a headline in a bad week. 

Start with the piece that moved overnight, because it is the one nobody is briefed on. Japan has been the world's supply of nearly free money for a generation - the place where you could borrow at essentially nothing and invest the proceeds anywhere else, which is the mechanism people mean when they say carry trade. This morning Takuji Aida, an economic adviser to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and a self-identified reflationist, said the Bank of Japan will likely raise rates in September and keep raising them once a quarter until the policy rate reaches 1.25% in January. The word reflationist matters: it means he is on the dovish side of the argument, the person you would expect to resist tightening. When the dove concedes, the debate is over. The yen moved immediately - USD/JPY fell 0.97% to 154.71, a six-month low for the dollar against the yen, and the euro and Australian dollar fell a comparable amount against it. 

Now set the other two beside it. Futures put the odds that the Federal Reserve RAISES rates on 16 September at roughly 57%, and - this is the number worth saying out loud to a client - the probability of a cut is exactly zero at every meeting priced through March 2027. Not low. Zero. The distribution contains no outcome below the current 3.50-3.75% target band. Separately, a Reuters poll published 3 September expects the European Central Bank to raise rates this Thursday for the second and final time in what would be its shortest tightening campaign in fifteen years. Treat that one as a forecast rather than a fact - the ECB has not decided - but the direction of the expectation is the point. 

Why this is genuinely useful rather than merely interesting: the price of money is the discount rate underneath every asset a client owns, and for fifteen years the marginal supplier of cheap money was Japan. If that supply is being withdrawn at the same time the Fed and the ECB are tightening, then the assumption that a market wobble will be met with easier policy - the assumption that has been correct since roughly 2009 - is not available right now. That is not a reason to sell anything. It is a reason to make sure the plan you built with a client does not quietly depend on rescue. 

The supply-side story sits underneath all of it and explains why the tightening is happening into visible weakness. Diesel set another high this morning: AAA's national average is $5.9015 a gallon, and AAA's own highest-recorded-average-price field now carries that exact figure dated 9/7/26, superseding the $5.8819 of two days ago. A year ago diesel averaged $3.7088 - a rise of 59.1%. Regular gasoline is $4.1505 against $3.1971 last September, up 29.8%, though regular is nowhere near its own high of $5.0165 from June 2022. Diesel matters more than gasoline even though clients notice gasoline first, because diesel moves freight and freight is embedded in the delivered price of nearly everything. And it is rising for a reason no central bank can fix: OPEC+ stopped adding barrels this weekend, and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to ten ships a day, the thinnest since May. Higher interest rates do not produce more diesel. If a client asks whether the Fed can do something about fuel prices, the accurate answer is: not quickly, and not directly. What it is defending is the expectation that inflation returns to target, which is why it may tighten into an energy shock even though that feels backwards. 

The practical counsel is patience about timing rather than any change in allocation. US markets have now been shut for three days. Everything above - the yen, OPEC+, the German election, the Kyiv talks, two days of Hormuz disruption - has had no US venue in which to be priced, and Tuesday's open is also the moment Canada's counter-tariffs on C$27.6bn of American goods take effect at 12:01 AM. That is a recipe for a session that looks more dramatic than it is, because it will compress three days of repricing into one. Then Friday brings the August CPI report, which the Fed has effectively named as the deciding input for its September vote, with the Committee already in blackout and unable to respond to it. Expect the noise, decline to trade it, and remember that one volatile session in a holiday-shortened week is not information about a long-term plan.
geo_headlines: THE YEN IS THE OVERNIGHT EVENT, AND IT HAS A NAMED CAUSE. USD/JPY fell to a six-month low, printing 154.71 at 11:04 UTC against Friday's 156.22 close - a decline of 0.971% - with an intraday low of 154.05 that broke through the 155.15 support level and tested the 24 February low. Daily RSI is around 27. The move was broad rather than dollar-specific: EUR/JPY fell 0.910% to 179.81 and AUD/JPY 0.791% to 111.65. The trigger is a single named comment. Takuji Aida, economic adviser to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and a self-identified reflationist, said Monday that the Bank of Japan is likely to hike in September and to continue hiking once a quarter through January 2027, reaching a 1.25% policy rate. The signal value comes from who said it: a dove inside the Prime Minister's own circle conceding the tightening is a different class of information from a hawkish forecaster predicting it. The Bank of Japan meets 17-18 September and prints its statement release time as undecided on its own schedule, so any specific clock time circulating for that decision is unsourced. No Bank of Japan official and no Ministry of Finance intervention comment was dated 6 or 7 September.

OPEC+ DECISION PUBLISHED - OCTOBER OUTPUT HELD AT SEPTEMBER LEVELS, AND THE SCOPE MATTERS. The group of eight met online Sunday and paused its run of monthly increases. The operative sentence, as quoted consistently by two independent outlets, is that the seven participating countries decided to maintain September 2026 required production for October 2026 as detailed in the statement table. October required production runs to roughly 31.01 million barrels a day combined: Saudi Arabia 10.478, Russia 9.949, Iraq 4.431, Kuwait 2.676, Kazakhstan 1.628, Algeria 1.007 and Oman 0.841. This ends four consecutive monthly increases of 188,000 barrels a day each for June, July, August and September, 752,000 cumulative. The group also reaffirmed full conformity with the Declaration of Cooperation and kept its monthly market reviews. Next meeting 4 October. TWO DISCIPLINE NOTES. First, 2027 quotas were NOT addressed in the published statement - some coverage framed the group as needing to agree new quotas before its next output step, but no 2027 baseline language appears in any version obtained, so yesterday's expectation that the focus would shift to 2027 is not confirmed. Second, a sourcing caveat stated plainly: opec.org refused automated retrieval and its cached press-release page is more than a year stale, so the wording above is a two-source quotation of the primary text rather than a direct read of the primary page.

IRAN AND HORMUZ - THE PHYSICAL DATA IS THE TRADEABLE PART. Kpler transit counts through the Strait of Hormuz fell to a 10-day moving average of 10 commodity ships a day as of Sunday, the lowest since May, down from above 15 on Friday; only two vessels physically transited Saturday and six Sunday, mostly on the Iranian route. That is throughput collapsing, measured rather than narrated, and it arrives in the same window as OPEC+ removing the supply-side offset. Iran's SNSC secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Sunday that Tehran will declare an exclusion zone outside Hormuz within days and place any ship entering it on an Iranian sanctions list, with the strait reopening only if the United States stops what he called sabotage, threats and attacks; the zone has been announced but not published. NO NEW US STRIKE WAS ANNOUNCED IN THIS WINDOW: CENTCOM's public releases page still tops out at the 5 September statement on the three IRGC tankers. An unreconciled claim conflict stands and is reported rather than resolved - Iran said Sunday it attacked a US unmanned vessel attempting to enter the strait, and CENTCOM denied Monday that any US vessel was struck. Tanker war-risk insurance premia and Gulf freight rates were checked and no dated 6-7 September print was obtainable, so any figure circulating this morning is unsourced.

SAXONY-ANHALT - AfD 43.8% ON A PRELIMINARY OFFICIAL COUNT, NO ABSOLUTE MAJORITY, AND MARKETS DID NOT CARE. These are preliminary official results with all 2,661 reporting units counted, not exit polls and not yet the legally certified tally: AfD 43.8%, CDU 17.2%, SPD 9.3%, Grüne 8.9%, Linke 8.6%, BSW 5.3% entering the Landtag, FDP 2.6% and out. Turnout was 77.8% against 60.3% in 2021, the highest since reunification. The arithmetic that matters is that AfD takes 39 seats and 42 are needed, so it has no absolute majority, and every other party maintains its refusal to enter coalition with it. FIGURE DISCIPLINE: the widely reported 44% is an exit-poll and mid-count extrapolation, not the completed preliminary official count of 43.8%; both circulate this morning and only the latter is the count. The new Landtag must convene by 6 October, no date is set for electing a Minister-President, and the outgoing CDU-SPD-FDP government stays in caretaker office having lost its majority. The market read is the useful part for clients: the euro was steady, the DAX was down 0.3%, and Frankfurt's own desk wrote flatly that the election played no role on the floor. Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern vote in two weeks.

KYIV READOUT PUBLISHED - NO FRAMEWORK, NO AGREEMENT, NO ANNOUNCED NEXT STEP. The Office of the President of Ukraine published statements at 22:39 on 6 September and 00:24 on 7 September following three rounds of talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Zelenskyy said difficult issues can only be resolved at the leaders' level, that there were several new ideas which he asked for an opportunity to analyse, and that Ukraine is counting heavily on a winter package if the war continues through winter - which he said is how it currently looks. Details were deliberately withheld, to be worked over the coming weeks with the United States and Europe. AP characterised the talks as encouraging but explicitly said they made no breakthrough. He named anti-ballistic capability as Ukraine's weak point and said 67 Ukrainian companies are working on jet-drone interception. THE PAUSE HELD FOR KYIV CITY ONLY, and the distinction is load-bearing: overnight Russia launched 92 strike drones and munitions, 71 were neutralised, and impacts were recorded at 12 locations including an infrastructure facility in Kyiv OBLAST, with no source reporting a strike on Kyiv city. Sunday's toll inside the pause was 4 dead in Kharkiv, 2 in Kyiv region, 2 in Kherson and 1 in Zaporizhzhia. The pause window itself is disputed - one account has it running three days from midnight on 6 September, another from 00:00 on 5 September to 23:59 on 8 September - and both are reported without averaging.

DIESEL AGAIN, AND THE PRIMARY SOURCE CARRIES IT. AAA's national average for diesel is $5.9015 a gallon on a page priced 9/7/26, and AAA's own highest-recorded-average-price field now reads exactly $5.9015 dated 9/7/26, superseding the $5.8819 of 9/5/26 that this brief shipped two days ago. So the high was reset inside this run's window, by the publisher's own data, for the second time in three days. Diesel is up $0.0045 on the day, $0.3013 on the week, $0.5702 on the month and $2.1927 on the year - the year-over-year rise is 59.1%. Regular gasoline is $4.1505 against $3.1971 a year ago, up 29.8%, and is nowhere near its own high of $5.0165 from 6/14/22. A CAVEAT AGAINST OVERSTATEMENT: mid-grade at $4.6325, premium at $5.0255 and E85 at $3.1268 each ticked DOWN day-over-day even as regular and diesel rose, so this morning is a mixed print rather than a uniform surge, and anyone writing pump prices rising should say which grade. Diesel is the number that matters for inflation transmission because it prices freight, and freight sits inside the delivered cost of nearly everything that arrives on a truck.

ASIA RALLIED HARD ON SEMICONDUCTORS, BUT THE BREADTH CONTRADICTS THE INDEX - DO NOT READ IT AS RISK-ON. The Nikkei 225 closed at 66,399.84, up 1,378.90 points or 2.12%, and the Kospi at 6,995.39, up 308.18 points or 4.61%. Hang Seng fell 0.93% to 25,413.12, the Shanghai Composite was about 0.2% lower near 3,920.70 and the ASX 200 was virtually unchanged at 9,005.30. The driver was semiconductors and AI, not macro: the largest Nikkei contributors were SoftBank Group, Advantest, Tokyo Electron, Kioxia and Ibiden. HERE IS THE PART WORTH CARRYING - beneath a 2.12% index gain, Tokyo Prime breadth was NEGATIVE, 630 advancers against 883 decliners, with only 17 of 33 sectors higher. That is a narrow, mega-cap-driven tape wearing the costume of a broad rally, and it matters for how you read Tuesday's US open, which inherits this lead unpriced. A VENDOR TRAP, FLAGGED NOT AVERAGED: wire copy circulating this morning gives the Nikkei at 66,104.93 and the Kospi at 6,907.53, which are intraday snapshots, and one European outlet cited 66,460.11, which is Tokyo's 11:30 JST lunch-break print mislabelled as a close. The settled closes are 66,399.84 and 6,995.39.

EUROPE DRIFTED LOWER ON OIL, NOT ON GERMANY, AND THE BOND PICTURE IS PARTLY UNVERIFIED. The DAX was down 0.3% at midday near 25,975 against Friday's 26,046 close, EuroStoxx 50 off 0.1% at 6,386, the CAC 40 up 0.09% at 8,285.85 and the broad STOXX 600 down 0.3%. Reuters attributed the softness to higher oil and Middle East risk rather than to the German result, with Novartis a named laggard. Gilts DID trade despite SIFMA recommending a full close for UK dollar-denominated fixed income: the 5-year gilt was quoted at 4.676%, up 4.7 basis points from a 4.630% previous close, last updated 08:08 BST, with gilt settlement running T+1. HONEST GAPS, STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER. No dated Monday Bund yield print was obtainable and no source reported a Bund move on the election, so the German curve level is unverified this morning. The JGB cash market is also unverified - Japan Bond Trading's reference-rate page had posted nothing after 3 September at time of check, even though Tokyo equities traded a normal session. And a UK 10-year vendor conflict is unresolved, with one source showing 4.88% for 9/4 and another 5.13%, most likely different series conventions, so no UK 10-year level should be quoted this morning without specifying which series.

VERIFIED NON-DEVELOPMENTS - EACH CHECKED, EACH PRODUCING NOTHING, ALL REPORTABLE. First and most consequential: no new statement from the President on the Federal Reserve, Chair Kevin Warsh, rates or trade is dated 6 or 7 September. The Truth Social archive shows a Sunday cluster between 11:54 AM and 7:09 PM ET whose captured content concerns a White House helipad; three post bodies did not render, so this is probable rather than certain silence. The live threat markets are still trading - the demand to lower the rate or halt trade with deficit countries - is dated Friday 4 September and is OUT OF WINDOW; weekend commentary recycling it is analysis, not news. Two days of presidential silence on the Fed going into a meeting the market has moved to pricing as a possible hike is itself the story. Second, no Chinese data was published: customs shows no August figures and the statistics bureau's newest item is dated 4 September. August trade is due Tuesday, where a Reuters poll of 35 economists expects exports up 25% year-over-year, imports up 30% and a surplus of $119.05bn - those are FORECASTS, not results. Third, no weekend change to Canada's counter-tariffs: no delay, carve-out or new ministerial comment is dated 6-7 September, so the measures are on track. Fourth, no Bank of Canada decision falls this week - its September fixed date was the 2nd, where it held at 2.25%.

REJECTED INPUT AND TWO CALENDAR CORRECTIONS - THE HOUSEKEEPING THAT KEEPS THIS BRIEF HONEST. First, a data artifact was caught and refused. Polygon served a daily bar dated 2026-09-07 for the VIX and for no other index. It MUTATED between two fetches minutes apart, first reading a close of 15.14 and then 15.17; its close equalled its high exactly; and no sibling bar exists for the S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, SOX, Dow or VXN. Since Cboe calculates VIX and VXN off the same session, a VIX print without a VXN print is not possible, and Cboe does not compute either on a US market holiday. The VIX tile therefore ships Friday's 14.53 settle. Shipping 15.17 would have invented a 4% volatility move on a day the options market was shut. Second, a correction in this brief's own favour: the FOMC press-conference time of 2:30 PM ET on 16 September IS published, as a discrete line item on the Federal Reserve's own September 2026 events calendar, alongside the 2:00 PM statement. Run #174 shipped that time as unverified; that was right on the evidence then available and is wrong now. Third, Oracle reports Thursday 10 September after the close, per its own investor-relations release - two aggregator pages assert 9 September and are wrong.
